changes: Rewrote bot driving behavior. Bots learn how to use brakes when necessary, slow down or accelerate based on incoming turns, avoid obstacles, and hard difficulty mode is a serious hard mode now.
Fixed a long-standing bug where when another vehicle crosses the finish line, the player would only hear it's sound and the sound would get cut completely instead of slowing down.
serverChanges: Fixed the console update on Linux and macOS failing at once with a message about a missing --pid argument. Versions 2026.8.9.12 and 2026.8.9.13 could not update themselves that way at all: nothing was replaced, the window waited five minutes, and the old server came back. A server on either of those versions has to be replaced by unpacking this one over it by hand. Windows, and any server installed as a service, were unaffected.

A server you started yourself on Linux or macOS now updates in the window you were already using, and comes back in it. Before, it looked as though it had died: the shell took the terminal back the moment the old server exited, so the new one arrived as a background process, which the system forbids from reading the terminal. It printed its banner and a prompt and then went quiet, while still running and still serving players. The updater's own output now appears in that window too. Windows is unchanged and still opens the updated server in a new console window.

Everything that waits for an update to finish now waits the same length of time. Three places watch for the file that marks an update in progress and each had its own answer, so a service could start a server while an update it should have waited for was still running. If you installed the service before this version, uninstall and install it again to pick that up: the waiting is written into the registration when the service is installed.

Installing the server as a service on Linux and macOS is now one command. Run it with sudo and --install-service and it does the whole job, registering the service to run as your account rather than root. Uninstall, start, stop and restart work the same way, and run without sudo they tell you the command to use, with the full path already filled in.

Installing the service now works on a machine where sudo was never set up. Debian offers a root password while it installs, and taking it leaves your own account out of the sudo group, so sudo fails there and su is the ordinary way to become root. Installing after su used to be refused, with advice to use a sudo that machine did not have. The account to register is now read from whoever owns the server folder, so it registers as you rather than as root.

On Linux the server now says where the service actually stands, because systemd will answer that without needing any rights. Service status reports whether it is installed, running and set to start with the machine, and any other service command typed without sudo tells you the status first and then the command that would change it. On macOS reading that needs root, so it still says so instead.

A Linux or macOS server that is already running as root now gets the full service menu, the same one Windows gets, instead of being told to use sudo. It has the rights already, which is the case where root is the only account on the machine.

Running the server itself as root is now refused on Linux and macOS, whether root was reached with sudo or with su. A server run that way left files in its folder that your own account could not replace, which showed up much later as settings that would not save or an update that would not install. It is decided by who owns the server folder rather than by how root was reached, so where root owns the folder and is the only account on the machine, which is common on a rented server, nothing is refused.

Fixed a second server started from a folder that already had one running taking over the folder instead of attaching to the server already there. Both then served the same port, the first could no longer be reached or shut down, and closing the newer one left the older one still answering.

The server no longer writes a desktop entry on Linux. No desktop environment will run one until you mark it trusted by hand, and that mark cannot be shipped with the file, so it failed silently rather than starting anything. The start-server.sh script, and Start Server.command on macOS, are unchanged.

Installing or removing the service on Linux and macOS no longer writes scripts to run afterwards. Running a script the server had just written was exactly as much work as running the server again with sudo, so there is now one way to do it and the server names the command.
